route

Liver most common, then peritoneum and lung; about half are metastatic at diagnosis.

Sources

Educational only, not medical advice. Schematic, not to scale: organ shapes, positions and sizes are illustrative, not anatomical. The routes show an ordering of where PDA spreads, taken from the sources; no per-organ percentages are implied. On a phone, tap a route button; hover or focus a part for a short explanation. Lymph nodes are regional spread, not a distant site. The local route covers growth along nerves into the retroperitoneum and the duodenum.

  • Distant spread. Liver is the principal distant site, reached through the portal vein; lung is the next hematogenous site: Pittman ME, Hruban RH, Pathology of Exocrine Pancreatic Tumors, in Beger et al., The Pancreas, 4th ed., 2023, ch. 125, pp. 958-959; Kumar V, Abbas AK, Aster JC, Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 9th ed., 2015, ch. 19, p. 894.
  • Peritoneal and lymphatic spread, and local extension. Peritoneal seeding (more with body/tail tumours), regional (peripancreatic) lymph nodes, and growth along nerves into the retroperitoneum and the duodenum: Robbins 9th ed. ch. 19, p. 894; Beger 2023 ch. 133, pp. 1033-1035. Perineural invasion is near-universal; vascular and lymphovascular invasion are common but variable: Beger 2023 ch. 125, pp. 958-959.
  • Usual sites and stage at diagnosis. Liver is the most common site, then peritoneum and lung; roughly 40-60% (about half) are metastatic at diagnosis: Kleeff J et al., Pancreatic cancer, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016;2:16022 (doi:10.1038/nrdp.2016.22); Beger 2023 ch. 134, p. 1037.

Left out / simplified: exact anatomy and relative positions, bone and other rarer sites, the portal venous anatomy, and any numeric per-site frequency (the sources give an ordering, not reliable percentages).
